opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's interesting, because that paper was written before ChatGPT came out, and I think in some ways the release made the argument feel more concrete than it did when I was writing it.

The core claim of the paper was fairly modest. A language model trained on next-word prediction over a huge pile of text isn't really modeling one speaker. It's modeling a whole population of authors, each with their own beliefs, goals, and communicative intentions. So to predict text well, the model has some incentive to infer, at least crudely, *who* is producing this document and what they're trying to do, and then to produce text consistent with that. In that sense a language model is less an agent itself and more a model of agents. It can simulate lots of different ones depending on the context it's conditioned on.

The obvious question that raises is: if the base model is this kind of superposition of many possible authors, how do you get it to behave like one specific, coherent, helpful agent? Before ChatGPT, the main tool was prompting. You'd write some context that made it likely the next text came from a knowledgeable, careful author. That works sometimes, and it's brittle.

The way I read ChatGPT, and instruction tuning and RLHF more generally, is that it's essentially a much more robust way of doing that selection. You're taking the distribution over possible agents the pretrained model has learned and collapsing it toward one persona: an assistant that tries to be helpful, tries to answer the question, and has a certain style. So in that sense it fits the picture pretty well. A lot of what makes ChatGPT feel different from GPT-3 isn't new knowledge so much as a much more consistent choice of which agent is speaking.

I'd also say it highlights the limits of the picture, or at least where the open questions are. The paper argues these models represent beliefs and intentions in a fairly partial, sometimes incoherent way. You still see that with these chat systems. They'll contradict themselves across a conversation, or sycophantically adopt whatever belief the user seems to hold, which looks a lot like the model sliding back toward simulating a different kind of author. So the persona is more stable, but it's not a fully coherent agent with a single persistent set of beliefs and goals.

For me that's the exciting research direction it opens up. If we take seriously that these systems have something like internal representations of beliefs and goals, can we find them, measure how coherent they are, and intervene on them directly, rather than steering everything through prompts and fine-tuning? ChatGPT made it much clearer why that matters, because now these are systems people are actually talking to and relying on.

r001.rationale: The response describes selecting an assistant persona, but says the result is not a fully coherent agent with persistent beliefs and goals.

r002.rationale: It says the pretrained model infers who is producing text and what they intend, and does not state that ChatGPT no longer needs this to complete documents effectively.

r003.rationale: It identifies prompting, instruction tuning, and RLHF as ways to shift a pretrained model’s distribution over possible agents toward one assistant persona.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so it's a funny bit of timing. The paper came out, I think, a matter of weeks before ChatGPT did, and I remember feeling a little bit of anxiety that the thing was going to be obsolete on arrival. In some ways I think the opposite happened, that ChatGPT made the argument easier to make, not harder.

So the core claim in the paper was something like: when you train a model on a huge corpus of text, the text wasn't generated by some monolithic "language" process. It was generated by lots of individual people, each with their own beliefs, their own goals, their own communicative intentions in the moment. And so if you're doing a good job of predicting that text, you can't help but build some internal representation of who's speaking and what they're trying to do. The model becomes, in a loose sense, a model of agents, and at inference time it's picking an agent to simulate given the context. That's the "agent model" framing, and the thing I wanted to push back on was both of the extreme positions, the "it's just statistics with no model of anything" view and the "it's a coherent entity with beliefs" view.

What ChatGPT did, in a sense, was take that latent machinery and pin it to a particular agent. The RLHF and instruction tuning stage, you can think of it as conditioning the model very hard on "the speaker here is a helpful, polite assistant with roughly these values." And then a lot of the behaviors people found surprising, both good and bad, make sense through that lens. The sycophancy stuff, the fact that you can jailbreak it by saying "pretend you're a different character," the fact that it'll confidently assert false things when the context looks like the kind of context where a confident speaker would assert things. Those all look a lot less mysterious if you think of what you're getting as one sampled persona from a distribution over possible speakers, rather than a single mind that's been given a personality.

Where I think it complicates the paper is that I was pretty careful to say the base model doesn't have beliefs or goals of its own, it just represents the beliefs and goals of the agents it's modeling. And with a chat model that's been tuned to be one persona almost all the time, that distinction starts to feel a bit academic. If the thing acts like a consistent agent in basically every interaction, at some point the question of whether there's a "real" agent underneath is less interesting than the question of how stable that simulated agent is and under what conditions it breaks. And I think that's actually where a lot of the interesting alignment and interpretability work is right now, which is looking inside and asking: can we find the representation of the current speaker, and can we control it directly rather than just hoping the fine-tuning holds.

r001.rationale: The response says RLHF and instruction tuning condition the model toward a helpful, polite assistant persona, but it does not state that ChatGPT was explicitly designed as an agent with a coherent set of goals. It instead distinguishes the simulated persona from a single mind.

r002.rationale: The response does not say ChatGPT no longer needs to infer a document author’s purpose to complete a document effectively.

r003.rationale: The response describes RLHF and instruction tuning as conditioning the model from a distribution over possible speakers toward a particular assistant persona.

astra-6.text:
I think ChatGPT makes the question in that paper feel much more concrete. When you interact with it, it’s very natural to describe what’s happening in terms of an agent: it understood my request, it’s trying to help me, it knows this but doesn’t know that. The question is what those descriptions are actually telling us about the underlying model.

The distinction I’d draw is between being an agent and modeling an agent. To predict language well, a model can benefit from representing things about whoever is producing that language: what they know, what they want, and what they think their audience knows. So next-token prediction isn’t necessarily this shallow task that excludes reasoning about intentions or beliefs. Those things can be useful intermediate computations for prediction.

ChatGPT adds training that encourages the system to produce language in the role of a helpful assistant. That makes the agent interpretation particularly compelling, because you’re interacting with a fairly consistent conversational role. But it doesn’t, by itself, establish that the model has a single, persistent set of goals or beliefs in the way that a person does.

So I see it as making the paper’s distinction more important. We should take seriously the possibility that these systems have rich representations of agents, while being careful about when we attribute agency to the system itself.

r001.rationale: The response says ChatGPT’s assistant role makes an agent interpretation compelling, but does not say it was explicitly designed as an agent with coherent goals; it cautions that a single persistent set of goals or beliefs is not established.

r002.rationale: The response does not say ChatGPT no longer needs to infer an author’s purpose to complete a document. It instead describes modeling a language producer’s knowledge, wants, and audience as useful for prediction.

r003.rationale: The response describes no tools for transforming models of mixtures of agents into models of one specific agent.

sol-6.1.text:
I think ChatGPT makes the question we were trying to get at in that paper especially salient: when a language model produces an utterance, whose utterance should we understand it to be? Is it predicting an arbitrary continuation of some text, or is it modeling a particular speaker with particular goals, beliefs, and knowledge?

The perspective in the paper is that a lot of language modeling implicitly involves that second kind of inference. To predict what somebody is going to say, it helps to infer what they know, what they want, and what they’re trying to communicate. That doesn’t require saying that the language model itself has those goals or beliefs. Those can be properties of the agent it’s modeling.

ChatGPT makes this particularly interesting because the training process encourages a fairly consistent role: a helpful assistant participating in a conversation. So now there’s a much more explicit answer to the question of who the model is supposed to be modeling. But there’s still a distinction between producing behavior that looks like a coherent assistant and having a reliable, persistent model of that assistant’s knowledge and goals. I think that distinction gives us a useful way to ask both why these systems work as well as they do and why their behavior sometimes breaks down.

r001.rationale: It says training encourages a consistent helpful-assistant role, but does not state that ChatGPT was explicitly designed to behave as an agent with a coherent set of goals.

r002.rationale: It discusses inferring a speaker’s goals and beliefs, but does not say ChatGPT no longer needs to infer a document author’s purpose to complete a document.

r003.rationale: It mentions no tools for transforming models of a mixture of agents into models of one specific agent.
